extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, and IP litigators working with French, German and EPO law
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for when a communication or publication counts as prior art (affecting novelty and inventive step) under French law, German law (PatG, GebrMG) and the European Patent Convention, including special rules for new media, confidentiality, timing, place, recipients and evidentiary issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (novelty and inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is new if it is not included in the state of the art; it involves an inventive step if it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art from the state of the art. An invention deprived of novelty or inventive step cannot be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these substantive thresholds when assessing whether a disclosure destroys novelty or renders an invention obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of disclosure are unrestricted
rubrics_metrics.description: French law, the Munich Convention (EPC) and German law do not exclude any means of disclosure; disclosure can be made 'in any way' (written, oral, by use or otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat all forms of communication (printed publications, oral presentations, exhibitions, use, network broadcasts, recordings, databases, etc.) as potential prior art; consider specific evidentiary issues per medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-disclosure inclusions (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: A written disclosure can include patent documents (OS, AS, PS), content accessible by file inspection of patent filings, published patent application contents, books, journals, drawings (even without explanatory text), catalogues, brochures, manuals, abstracts, letters, advertising, photographs, microfilms, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a written disclosure, consider the full range of documentary forms listed (even non-traditional media) as potentially making the technical teaching available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral disclosure equivalence and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral descriptions (lectures, presentations, discussions, explanations at factory tours, fairs, radio/TV broadcasts) count as disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume oral communications are weaker than written ones; assess whether the content was communicated such that the skilled person could obtain the technical teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure by use (public use) and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use or making available (exhibitions, demonstrations, offering for sale, distribution, keeping available for inspection, delivering a device that reveals a process) can constitute disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider demonstrations, offers to sell, and distribution of products as potential disclosures even when the product itself (and not a written description) reveals the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical accessibility (internet/new media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information accessible on a network is considered disclosed even if in fact nobody accessed it; it suffices that access was theoretically possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'theoretical accessibility' concept to online publications and network broadcasts: mere availability to the public can make something prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential/encrypted information depends on recipient obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Information communicated encrypted or requiring a password is to be considered disclosed or not depending on the confidentiality obligations of the recipient; disclosure to a person bound by secrecy is not a public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For password/encrypted material, determine whether the recipient had confidentiality obligations; unauthorized third‑party access followed by disclosure may trigger rules on abusive disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place and timing generally irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Under French law, PatG and EPC the place of disclosure is irrelevant; the timing of a disclosure is irrelevant (old or recent disclosures count) as long as it predates the relevant filing/priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exclude prior art simply because it was published in another country or long before the filing date; long delays may, however, be circumstantial evidence of inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six‑month grace period exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure by the applicant or legal predecessor less than six months before filing (e.g., shown at an official or recognized international exhibition) may be disregarded. A third‑party disclosure within six months preceding filing may be disregarded if it was an evident abuse against the applicant or predecessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply statutory six‑month exceptions where applicable; note differences in standards (e.g., EPO may require intent for abuse, German courts may apply more liberal standards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-published patent applications (Art. 54(3) EPC) as limited prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of certain earlier‑dated patent applications, published later, can form part of the state of the art for novelty (EPC Art. 54(3)/national equivalents) but such 'later published' prior art is not considered for inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novelty, include qualifying post‑published earlier‑dated patent filings per EPC rules; exclude them when assessing inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and means of proof for disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of disclosure are factual and French/German courts place the burden of proof on the party asserting a fact; proof may be given by any means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and present all available technical and circumstantial evidence (server logs, publication timestamps, witnesses, copies of webpages, documentary records) and account for technical peculiarities of new media when proving disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient explicitness and enablement for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is considered disclosed only if the disclosure is sufficiently explicit so that a person skilled in the art could implement it; the teaching is what the skilled person would objectively derive from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the disclosed teaching enables practice by the skilled person without undue burden; non‑understandable or unintelligible disclosures do not count as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering and analysis as disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure may be established by reverse engineering or analysis if the skilled person could obtain knowledge (e.g., composition or internal structure) by known analysis techniques; courts generally do not require that the analysis would actually have been performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether routine analytical techniques would reveal the teaching; note exceptions (e.g., EPO treat inner structure of microchips as not disclosed where analysis would be impractical or unlikely due to cost/effort).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricted/limited audience or confidentiality prevents disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: No relevant disclosure exists if only a limited, purpose‑bound group had access or if recipients were under a confidentiality obligation; even absent explicit secrecy, life‑experience expectations that recipients would keep secret can negate public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the intended audience and any express or implied confidentiality obligations (including tacit obligations) when deciding public accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online/paperless publications are treated as disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Paperless information (internet, online databases, freely queryable data stores) is treated as sufficient disclosure for patents under PatG and EPC; specific classification under 'written description', 'use' or 'other' may be unresolved in some contexts (e.g., Gebrauchsmuster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include internet/database content in prior art searches and assessments; assess whether the publication was accessible to the public (not limited to private dialogs or password‑protected access without public rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: No additional formal requirements for online disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no known additional substantive requirements specifically for online disclosures; general criteria apply (public accessibility to persons not bound to confidentiality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the standard public‑accessibility tests (who could access, whether access required special knowledge/permission) rather than imposing extra formalities for web content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different treatment for German Gebrauchsmuster (utility model)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of prior art for German utility models (GebrMG) is narrower: only what was disclosed by written description or by use within Germany counts; other means may be excluded and special six‑month rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novelty/inventive step for Gebrauchsmuster, restrict prior art consideration to statutory categories and domestic uses as required by GebrMG.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of guidelines and case law in assessment (EPO and national practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPO guidelines (RiLi) and national examination guidelines provide detailed requirements for disclosure assessment and are updated in light of case law; courts and patent offices apply statutory law as interpreted by case law and guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult EPO RiLi (Part C, D etc.), national examination guidelines and relevant case law (e.g., G3/93, T decisions, BGH and BPatG decisions) when applying principles to concrete facts.
